title: Graphs that tell a story
objectives: Read a distance-time graph as a journey and a cost graph as a bill
Interpret the gradient of a graph as a rate of change, with units
Tell the height of a graph apart from its gradient

screens.title: Graphs that tell a story
screens.prose: A graph of distance against time is a record of a journey. Its height says where you are. Its steepness says how fast you are going.
Sam walks from home to a shop, then walks back. The graph shows Sam's distance from home over 25 minutes.
screens.question: What is Sam doing between 10 and 15 minutes?

options.text: Standing still at the shop
Walking at a steady speed
options.why: You read the flat line as steady progress. Flat means the distance from home is not changing.

options.text: Walking home
options.why: Walking home makes the distance shrink, so the graph would go down. Here it stays at 800 m.

options.text: Walking fastest, because the graph is highest
options.why: You read height as speed. Height is distance from home, and here it is not changing at all.

hints.text: What does the height of the graph measure?
Look at the flat stretch at the top.
From 10 to 15 minutes the distance stays at 800 m. Sam is not getting nearer or further.

feedback.correct: The distance holds at 800 m: Sam is at the shop.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the height measures, then what a flat stretch means.

explain.text: Height is distance from home. A flat stretch means the distance is not changing, so Sam is standing still 800 m from home: at the shop.

screens.prose: A car pulls away from a junction. After $t$ seconds it has gone $d = t^2$ metres. The line touching the curve at P shows the **gradient** there. Move P with the slider.
screens.question: What happens to the gradient as time goes on?

options.text: It increases: the curve gets steeper
It stays the same, because the car keeps moving
options.why: A steady gradient would make a straight line. Watch the gradient label as you slide.

options.text: It equals the height of P
options.why: At $t = 3$ the height is 9 but the gradient is 6. Height and gradient are different readings.

hints.text: Slide P from left to right and watch the label on the touching line.
Compare the gradient at $t = 1$ with the gradient at $t = 5$.
At $t = 1$ the label reads 2; at $t = 5$ it reads 10. The curve gets steeper.

feedback.correct: The curve steepens, so the gradient grows.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide P and read the gradient at a few times.

explain.text: The gradient grows from 2 at $t = 1$ to 10 at $t = 5$. A steeper graph means distance is piling up faster: the car is speeding up.

screens.prose: The gradient at a point measures how fast the height is changing there: its **rate of change**. Here it is metres per second, the car's speed.
screens.question: Drag P to $t = 3$. How fast is the car going at that moment?

hints.text: Speed is the gradient at P, not its height.
Read the label on the touching line when P is at $t = 3$.
At $t = 3$ the touching line has gradient 6: the car is doing 6 m/s.

feedback.correct: The gradient at $t = 3$ is 6, so the car is doing 6 m/s.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the gradient of the touching line at $t = 3$.

byKey.avg: You divided 9 m by 3 s. That is the average speed since the start; at $t = 3$ the car is already going faster.
byKey.height: 9 m is how far the car has gone. The speed is the gradient at P, not its height.

explain.text: At $t = 3$ the touching line climbs 6 m per second, so the speed is 6 m/s. The average since the start, $9 \div 3 = 3$ m/s, is lower because the car began slowly.

screens.prose: Back to Sam's walk. On a straight stretch the gradient is the same everywhere: rise over run between any two points.
screens.question: What is the gradient of the graph between 15 and 25 minutes?

hints.text: Rise over run from A to B. Is the rise up or down?
From A to B the graph drops.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the change in distance by the change in time, keeping the sign.

byKey.pos: You gave Sam's speed, 80 m per minute. The distance is falling, so the gradient is negative: −80.
byKey.rise: You found the change in distance, −800 m, but not the time it took. Divide by the 10 minutes.

explain.text: The graph falls 800 m over 10 minutes: $\dfrac{-800}{10} = -80$ metres per minute. The minus sign says Sam is heading home. The speed is 80 m per minute either way.

screens.prose: An energy tariff charges £0.30 a unit for the first 100 units each month, then a lower rate. The graph shows the monthly bill against units used.
screens.question: After the first 100 units, what does each extra unit cost?

hints.text: The cost of each extra unit is the gradient after 100 units.
Use A and B: both are past 100 units.
From A to B the bill rises £20.00 over 100 units: $20 \div 100 = 0.20$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the gradient between A and B.

byKey.avg: You divided £50.00 by 200 units. That is the average cost per unit, which mixes in the dearer first 100.
byKey.first: £0.30 is the rate for the first 100 units. After A the graph is less steep.

explain.text: After 100 units the bill rises £20.00 for every 100 units, so the gradient is £0.20 a unit. The average, £50.00 ÷ 200 = £0.25, is the gradient of the dashed line from the origin to B.

screens.prose: Now go from story to graph. Jo jogs away from home at 100 m a minute for 2 minutes, rests for 1 minute, then jogs straight home at the same speed.
screens.question: Drag the six points to sketch Jo's distance from home.

hints.text: Where is Jo after 1 minute? After 2? After the rest?
The curve you drag is the sketch.
Heights at 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 minutes: 0, 100, 200, 200, 100 and 0 metres.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out Jo's distance from home at each whole minute.

byKey.home-up: Your graph keeps climbing after the rest. Jogging home makes the distance from home shrink, so the graph comes back down.

explain.text: Steady jogging gives straight sloping stretches: gradient 100 on the way out and −100 on the way back. The rest is flat. The graph ends at 0 because Jo ends at home.

screens.prose: A share's price over a morning follows this curve. At 3 hours it reaches its high of £109.00. A trader says: "It is at its highest, so it is still rising."
screens.question: Drag P to the high. What is true of the gradient there?

options.text: It is 0: the price is level for an instant, rising before and falling after
It is largest there, because the price is highest
options.why: You read height as gradient. The price rose fastest at the open, at £100.00, where the graph is steepest.

options.text: It is positive, because the price has not fallen yet
options.why: Just after 3 hours the price is below £109.00. A price that is still rising would go higher.

options.text: It is negative, because the price is about to fall
options.why: It falls only after the top. At the top itself the touching line is flat.

hints.text: Drag P to the top and look at the touching line.
Read the gradient label at the high.
At $t = 3$ the touching line is flat: gradient 0. Before, it is positive; after, negative.

feedback.correct: Correct. At the high the gradient is 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag P to the top and read the gradient there.

byKey.b: You took the highest point to be the steepest. Height says how much; gradient says how fast. At the top the gradient is 0.
byKey.c: You reasoned that a price still at its high must still be rising. Rising means the next moment is higher, and here it is lower.

explain.text: Height and gradient answer different questions: how high, and how fast it is changing. At the high the touching line is flat, gradient 0. The price rose fastest at the open, when it was lowest.

screens.prose: In every story the height said **how much** and the gradient said **how fast**. $$\text{gradient} = \frac{\text{change in } y}{\text{change in } x}$$ Its units are $y$-units per $x$-unit, such as metres per minute or pounds per unit. A flat stretch means no change.
screens.question: A graph shows a fund's value in pounds against time in days. At one point its gradient is −250. What does that mean?

options.text: At that moment the fund is losing about £250.00 a day
The fund is worth −£250.00
options.why: You read the gradient as a height. A gradient is a rate: pounds per day.

options.text: The fund has lost £250.00 in total
options.why: A gradient is the change per day at that moment, not the total change since the start.

feedback.correct: −250 pounds per day: falling at £250.00 a day.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the units: pounds per day.

screens.prose: A strategy's cumulative P&L at the end of each day, starting from £0.00 on day 0. A **drawdown** is a fall from a peak to a later trough.
screens.question: What is the largest drawdown, in pounds?

hints.text: Find the highest point before the curve dips.
The P&L line peaks on day 3, then falls for three days.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take a peak, then the lowest point after it.

byKey.max-min: You took the lowest value from the highest. But the £420.00 high comes after the trough, so that fall never happened.
byKey.trough: £90.00 is the level at the trough. The drawdown is the fall to it from the peak before.

explain.text: The P&L peaks at £310.00 on day 3 and bottoms out at £90.00 on day 6, a trough. The drawdown is £220.00. At the trough the gradient turns from negative to positive, like a lowest turning point.

ideas: The height of a graph says how much; its gradient says how fast that amount is changing.
A gradient has units: $y$-units per $x$-unit, such as metres per minute or pounds per unit.
At a highest or lowest point the gradient is 0, however high or low the graph is.

formula.name: Rate of change
formula.note: On a curve, use the line that touches the graph at the point.

summary.trap: A graph at its highest is not still rising: at the top the gradient is 0.

quiz.prose: A distance-time graph has a horizontal stretch.
quiz.question: What does that stretch mean?

options.text: Standing still
Moving at a steady speed
options.why: Steady speed gives a straight sloping line. Flat means the distance is not changing.

options.text: Moving at top speed
options.why: You read the stretch as fast. A flat graph has gradient 0: speed 0.

feedback.correct: Gradient 0 means no change in distance.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the gradient of a flat line is.

explain.text: A horizontal stretch has gradient 0. The distance does not change, so the traveller is standing still.

quiz.prose: A tank's volume falls in a straight line from 600 litres at 0 minutes to 240 litres at 12 minutes.
quiz.question: What is the gradient of its volume-time graph, in litres per minute?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the change in volume by the change in time.

byKey.pos: The volume is falling, so the gradient is negative: −30.
byKey.rise: −360 litres is the change in volume. Divide by the 12 minutes it took.

explain.text: The volume changes by $240 - 600 = -360$ litres in 12 minutes. The gradient is $-360 \div 12 = -30$ litres per minute: the tank drains at 30 litres a minute.

quiz.prose: A strategy's cumulative P&L over five days.
quiz.question: Between which two days did the P&L fall fastest?

options.text: Days 2 and 3
Days 3 and 4
options.why: You picked where the P&L reached its low. It fell only £20.00 then; from day 2 to 3 it fell £80.00.

options.text: Days 1 and 2
options.why: P&L rose then, by £50.00. A slower rise is still a rise.

feedback.correct: −£80.00 in one day: the steepest fall.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the day-to-day change that is most negative.

explain.text: The daily changes are +£150.00, +£50.00, −£80.00, −£20.00 and +£60.00. The steepest downward stretch is day 2 to day 3, even though the low comes a day later.

quiz.prose: A car has gone $d = t^2$ metres after $t$ seconds.
quiz.question: What is its average speed over the first 4 seconds, in m/s?

feedback.correct: 16 m in 4 s: 4 m/s on average.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the distance gone by the time taken.

byKey.inst: 8 m/s is the speed at the moment $t = 4$, the gradient there. The average over the whole time is lower.
byKey.dist: 16 m is the distance gone. Divide by the 4 seconds.

explain.text: After 4 seconds the car has gone $4^2 = 16$ m. The average speed is $16 \div 4 = 4$ m/s, the gradient of the straight line from the origin to $(4, 16)$.
